title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 27: Didipio v. Gozun: Constitutionality of the Mining Act: A Reprise
keywords: La Bugal-B'laan Tribal Association v. Ramos
agreements involving either technical or financial assistance
primary_topics: Chapter 27 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- a digest of Didipio v. Gozun, a reprise of the mining-law controversy in which the Court, through Justice Minita V. Chico-Nazario, brushed aside the procedural objections and answered every substantive challenge to the Philippine Mining Act of 1995 and its implementing rules in the negative.

The eminent domain question: Section 76 of Republic Act 7942 is a taking provision, but a valid one, because mining is an industry that yields public benefit and the law and its rules provide for the payment of just compensation.

The preservation of judicial power over just compensation: the panel of arbitrators may make only a preliminary determination, while the original and exclusive jurisdiction of the courts remains intact.

The reaffirmation of La Bugal-B'laan: the State retains more than sufficient control over mining operations, the phrase 'agreements involving either technical or financial assistance' is not confined to mere assistance, and service contracts were not eradicated by the 1987 Constitution.
sub_topics: On June 20, 1994, before the passage of the Mining Act, President Fidel V. Ramos executed an FTAA with Arimco Mining Corporation over some 37,000 hectares in Nueva Vizcaya and Quirino, including Barangay Didipio in Kasibu.
Arimco consolidated with Climax Mining Limited into Climax-Arimco Mining Corporation, 99 percent of whose controlling stockholders were Australian nationals.

On September 7, 2001 counsels for petitioners demanded from DENR Secretary Heherson Alvarez the cancellation of the CAMC FTAA on the ground that Republic Act 7942 and DAO 96-40 were unconstitutional; the Mines and Geosciences Bureau panel of arbitrators rejected the demand, and the present Petition for Prohibition and Mandamus followed.

The issues were split into a procedural set -- whether eminent domain presented a justiciable controversy and whether petitioners had legal standing -- and a substantive set on unlawful taking, judicial power over just compensation, State control, the reach of technical or financial assistance agreements, and the legality of service contracts.

On ripeness, the Court found a live controversy because the law had been enacted, the order approved and FTAAs entered into, with holders already operating in several provinces and petitioners in danger of being ousted from their landholdings; actual eviction did not have to happen first.
Legal standing was affirmed, petitioners having alleged personal and substantial injury from the mining activities and an imminent threat of displacement.

On the merits, the history of mining laws showed that qualified operators were granted authority to exercise eminent domain for entry into and use of private lands, and since Section 1 of PD 512 was deemed incorporated in Section 76, that section was a taking provision.

That conclusion did not make Section 76 unconstitutional: the mining industry was deemed pivotal to economic development and a vital tool in accelerated recovery, so the taking was for public use, and just compensation was provided for.

The claim that the CAMC FTAA contractually reduced the State's discretion to take was rejected; the agreement merely set out how a foreign contractor disqualified from owning land could identify surface areas for the government to acquire by voluntary transaction, shielding it from an Anti-Dummy Law charge.
Eminent domain was not yet called for at that stage, since surface rights could still be acquired by means other than expropriation.

On judicial power, the Court held that the Mining Act did not bar courts from taking cognizance of expropriation cases: Section 107 contemplated a voluntary transaction, and even where the arbitrators determine compensation for an involuntary taking, the determination is only preliminary unless accepted by all parties.

On State control, the Court invoked La Bugal-B'laan to hold that the contractor was not free to do whatever it pleased, and that the law and its implementing rules vested in the government more than a sufficient degree of control and supervision.

On the meaning of 'agreements involving either technical or financial assistance', the word 'involving' implied that such agreements were not limited to mere financial and technical assistance; had the framers meant to confine foreign participation, their language would have been unmistakably restrictive and stringent.

On service contracts, the deletion of the 1973 Charter's term from the 1987 Constitution did not amount to a ban; the present Charter still allows such contracts with foreign corporations that invest in and operate extractive enterprises under the full control of the State, this time with safety measures against the abuses of the past regime.

stances.claim: The controversy was ripe and the petitioners had standing, because the law had been enacted, the implementing order approved and FTAAs entered into, leaving numerous residents in danger of being ousted from their landholdings -- actual eviction did not have to happen before the Court could intervene.
stances.rhetorical_move: clearing procedural underbrush by treating imminent displacement as a present clash of legal rights

stances.claim: Section 76 of Republic Act 7942 is a taking provision, since the authority of qualified mining operators to exercise eminent domain under PD 512 is deemed incorporated in it, but it is not unconstitutional because mining yields public benefit and the law provides for just compensation.
stances.rhetorical_move: conceding the characterization the petitioners urged, then defeating the conclusion they drew from it

stances.claim: The Mining Act does not encroach on judicial power, because the panel of arbitrators makes only a preliminary determination of compensation unless all parties accept it, while the original and exclusive jurisdiction of the courts to determine just compensation remains intact.
stances.rhetorical_move: distinguishing voluntary from involuntary transactions and recasting the administrative determination as provisional

stances.claim: The State retains more than a sufficient degree of control and supervision over mining operations, the phrase 'agreements involving either technical or financial assistance' is not confined to mere assistance, and service contracts survive under the 1987 Constitution with safeguards against past abuses -- all as already settled in La Bugal-B'laan.
stances.rhetorical_move: reliance on a recent controlling precedent, reinforced by close reading of the word 'involving' and of the framers' deliberate choice of unrestrictive language

notable_anecdotes: A 1994 agreement signed before the Mining Act even existed put 37,000 hectares of Nueva Vizcaya and Quirino -- including the barangay of Didipio that gave the case its name -- under a single mining agreement.
The foreign character of the venture was stark: after Arimco consolidated with Climax Mining Limited, 99 percent of the controlling stockholders of the resulting company were Australian nationals.

The residents' challenge began not in court but with a demand letter to the DENR secretary, which was referred to a regional panel of arbitrators in Tuguegarao and rejected there before the Petition was filed.

The Court refused to wait for the bulldozers: it held that it could not await the adverse consequences of the law, and that actual eviction of landowners and occupants did not have to happen before it would intervene.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 27 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Didipio v. Gozun, a reprise of the mining-law controversy, in which the Court through Justice Minita V. Chico-Nazario brushed aside the procedural objections and answered all the substantive questions in the negative. On June 20, 1994, before the Philippine Mining Act of 1995 was passed, President Fidel V. Ramos executed a Financial and Technical Assistance Agreement with Arimco Mining Corporation covering some 37,000 hectares in Nueva Vizcaya and Quirino, including Barangay Didipio in Kasibu; Arimco later consolidated with Climax Mining Limited into a company 99 percent of whose controlling stockholders were Australian nationals. After a demand letter to the DENR secretary was referred to and rejected by the Mines and Geosciences Bureau panel of arbitrators, residents petitioned for prohibition and mandamus to have Republic Act 7942 and DAO 96-40 declared unconstitutional and the FTAA cancelled. The Court held the controversy ripe, since the law had been enacted, the order approved and agreements entered into, with petitioners in danger of being ousted from their landholdings; actual eviction did not have to happen before it would intervene, and their standing was likewise affirmed. On the merits it held that Section 76 was a taking provision, the eminent domain authority of qualified operators under PD 512 being deemed incorporated in it, but that the taking was valid because the mining industry was pivotal to economic development and yielded public benefit, and because just compensation was provided for. The claim that the agreement contractually reduced the State's discretion was rejected, the FTAA merely facilitating the government's voluntary acquisition of surface areas for a contractor disqualified from owning land. The Mining Act did not encroach on the courts' power over just compensation, since an arbitral determination is only preliminary unless accepted by all parties. Citing La Bugal-B'laan, the Court held that the State retained more than sufficient control over mining operations, that 'agreements involving either technical or financial assistance' were not limited to mere assistance, and that service contracts were not eradicated by the 1987 Constitution but continue under full State control with safety measures against past abuses.
